objective.statement: Say how the sound of an instrument is made: a single reed, a double reed, air across an edge, buzzing lips or plucked strings.
successCriteria: I know the clarinet family uses one reed.
I know the oboe family and the bassoon family use two reeds.
I know brass players buzz their lips into a mouthpiece.

explanation.text: Instruments make their sound in different ways. In the woodwind family most instruments use a reed, a thin piece of cane that vibrates when air passes it. The clarinet and the bass clarinet use a single reed. The oboe, the cor anglais, the bassoon and the double bassoon use two reeds that vibrate against each other: a double reed. (The saxophone, which is not a regular member of the orchestra, uses a single reed.)

The flute and the piccolo have no reed. The player blows air across an opening, as you do across the top of a bottle; the recorder is blown through a mouthpiece against an edge. Brass instruments are different again: the player's lips buzz into a mouthpiece, and the shape of the tube (and, on a trombone, a slide) changes the pitch.

The harp is a string instrument: its strings are plucked with the fingers. It has been used in the orchestra since the Romantic period, but it is not counted as part of the orchestra's string section.
One reed: clarinets and saxophone. Two reeds: oboe, cor anglais, bassoons. No reed: flute, piccolo, recorder. Buzzing lips: brass. Plucked: harp.

steps: Think of the instrument: the oboe.
Its player blows between two reeds.
So the oboe is a double reed instrument.
demonstration.textAlternative: A short phrase; the oboe is a double reed instrument.
